title: No. 75 — The Treaty-Making Power of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President is to have power, "by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur." Though this provision has been attacked, on different grounds, with no small vehemence, I do not hesitate to declare my firm conviction that it is one of the best digested and most unobjectionable parts of the plan. One ground of objection is the trite topic of the intermixture of powers. Some contend that the President alone should hold the power of making treaties, while others say it should have been deposited exclusively in the Senate. Another source of objection is drawn from the small number of persons by whom a treaty may be made. Of those who hold this objection, some think the House of Representatives should have been associated in the business, while others seem to think that nothing more was needed than to substitute two-thirds of all the members of the Senate for two-thirds of the members present. As I flatter myself that the observations made in a preceding number on this part of the plan must have been enough to place it in a very favorable light to a discerning eye, I shall here content myself with offering only some supplementary remarks, mainly aimed at the objections just stated.

Regarding the intermixture of powers, I shall rely on the explanations already given elsewhere of the true sense of the rule on which that objection is founded. I shall take it for granted, as an inference from them, that the union of the Executive with the Senate in the matter of treaties is no infringement of that rule. I venture to add that the particular nature of the treaty-making power suggests a special propriety in that union. Though several writers on government place that power in the class of executive authorities, this is plainly an arbitrary classification. If we attend carefully to its operation, it will be found to partake more of the legislative than of the executive character, though it does not strictly fall within the definition of either. The essence of legislative authority is to enact laws — to prescribe rules for regulating society. Executing the laws and employing the common strength, either for that purpose or for the common defense, seem to comprise all the functions of the executive magistrate. The power to make treaties is plainly neither of these. It does not relate to the execution of existing laws, nor to the enactment of new ones, and still less to an exertion of the common strength. Its objects are CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law but derive it from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules prescribed by the sovereign to the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign. The power in question therefore seems to form a distinct department, properly belonging neither to the legislative nor to the executive. The qualities described elsewhere as indispensable in the management of foreign negotiations point to the Executive as the most fit agent in those transactions, while the vast importance of the trust, and the operation of treaties as laws, plead strongly for the participation of all or part of the legislative body in the making of them.

However proper or safe it may be in governments where the executive magistrate is a hereditary monarch to commit to him the entire treaty-making power, it would be wholly unsafe and improper to entrust that power to an elective magistrate of four years' duration. It has been observed elsewhere, and the observation is unquestionably just, that a hereditary monarch — though often the oppressor of his people — has personally too much stake in the government to be in any serious danger of being corrupted by foreign powers. But a man raised from the station of a private citizen to the rank of chief magistrate, possessing a moderate or slender fortune, and looking forward to a not very distant time when he may probably have to return to the station from which he was taken, might sometimes be under temptations to sacrifice his duty to his interest that would require superlative virtue to resist. An avaricious man might be tempted to betray the interests of the state for the acquisition of wealth. An ambitious man might make his own aggrandizement, with the aid of a foreign power, the price of his treachery to his constituents. The history of human conduct does not warrant the exalted opinion of human virtue that would make it wise in a nation to commit interests so delicate and momentous as those concerning its dealings with the rest of the world to the sole disposal of a magistrate situated as a President of the United States would be.

To have entrusted the treaty-making power to the Senate alone would have been to give up the benefits of the constitutional involvement of the President in the conduct of foreign negotiations. It is true that the Senate would in that case have the option of employing him in this capacity. But it would also have the option of leaving him out, and pique or cabal might lead to the latter rather than the former. Besides this, the ministerial servant of the Senate could not be expected to enjoy the confidence and respect of foreign powers to the same degree as the constitutional representative of the nation, and so would not be able to act with equal weight or effectiveness. While the Union would, for this reason, lose a considerable advantage in managing its external concerns, the people would lose the additional security that would result from the cooperation of the Executive. Though it would be imprudent to confide such an important trust to him alone, it cannot be doubted that his participation would materially add to the safety of society. It must indeed be clear to a demonstration that joint possession of this power by the President and Senate would offer greater prospects of security than separate possession by either of them. And whoever has carefully weighed the circumstances that must come together in the appointment of a President will be satisfied that the office will always be likely to be filled by men of such character as to make their concurrence in the formation of treaties especially desirable, both on the score of wisdom and of integrity.

The remarks made in a former number, alluded to in another part of this paper, will apply with conclusive force against admitting the House of Representatives to a share in the formation of treaties. The fluctuating composition of that body, and — taking its future increase into account — its very large size, forbid us to expect in it the qualities essential to the proper execution of such a trust. Accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics; steady and systematic adherence to the same views; a delicate and uniform sensibility to national character; decision, secrecy, and dispatch — these are incompatible with the spirit of a body so variable and so numerous. The very complexity of the business, by requiring the concurrence of so many different bodies, would itself form a solid objection. The greater frequency of calls on the House of Representatives, and the greater length of time it would often be necessary to keep them together when convened, to obtain their approval at progressive stages of a treaty, would be a source of such great inconvenience and expense as alone ought to condemn the proposal.

The only objection that remains to be examined is the one that would substitute two-thirds of all the members of the Senate for two-thirds of the members present. It has been shown, under the second head of our inquiries, that all provisions requiring more than a majority of any body for its resolutions have a direct tendency to embarrass the operations of government, and an indirect one to subject the sense of the majority to that of the minority. This consideration seems enough to settle our opinion that the convention has gone as far as could be reconciled with the activity of the public councils or with a reasonable regard for the majority sense of the community in trying to secure the advantage of numbers in the formation of treaties. If two-thirds of the whole number of members had been required, it would, in many cases — because of the non-attendance of some — amount in practice to a necessity of unanimity. And the history of every political establishment where this principle has prevailed is a history of impotence, perplexity, and disorder. Proofs of this could be drawn from the examples of the Roman Tribuneship, the Polish Diet, and the States-General of the Netherlands — were it not that an example at home renders foreign precedents unnecessary.

Requiring a fixed proportion of the whole body would not, in all probability, contribute to the advantages of a numerous body any better than merely requiring a proportion of the attending members. The first, by always requiring a determinate number for a resolution, lessens the motives for punctual attendance. The second, by making the capacity of the body depend on a proportion that may vary with the absence or presence of a single member, has the opposite effect. And since, by promoting punctuality, it tends to keep the body complete, there is great likelihood that its resolutions would generally be dictated by as large a number in the latter case as in the former, while there would be far fewer occasions of delay. It ought not to be forgotten that under the existing Confederation, two members may, and usually do, represent a state. As a result, Congress — which is now solely invested with all the powers of the Union — rarely consists of a greater number of persons than would compose the proposed Senate. If we add that the members vote by states, and that where only a single member from a state is present, his vote is lost, it justifies the supposition that the active votes in the Senate, where members are to vote individually, would rarely fall short in number of the active votes in the present Congress. When, in addition to these considerations, we take into view the cooperation of the President, we shall not hesitate to infer that the people of America would have greater security against an improper use of the treaty-making power under the new Constitution than they now enjoy under the Confederation. And when we go a step further and look forward to the probable enlargement of the Senate by the erection of new states, we shall not only see ample ground for confidence in the sufficiency of those to whom that power is entrusted, but we shall probably be led to conclude that a body more numerous than the Senate is likely to become would be very little fit for the proper discharge of the trust.
